items.title: 14.4 Simple Harmonic Motion and Uniform Circular Motion

source_refs.note: Topic 14.4 with Example 14.3 and the box (PDF 25-28); Figs 14.4-14.7 are redrawn in one figure. The misprinted equation 14.13 and the sign of v are noted.

blocks.text: S.H.M. can be understood by relating it to uniform circular motion. When a particle moves round a circle at constant speed, its projection on a diameter of the circle executes S.H.M. Consider a turntable of radius r with a ball attached to its rim; a beam of light casts a shadow of the ball on a screen (Fig 14.4). When the turntable rotates with constant angular speed w, the ball moves in uniform circular motion and its shadow moves to and fro across the screen in S.H.M., like a body on a spring.

blocks.alt: Light from a projector shines down on a turntable with a ball fixed to its rim; a curved arrow shows the circular motion of the ball. Below, on a screen, the ball's shadow moves to and fro, marked oscillation of ball's shadow.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.4: The oscillation of the shadow of ball on screen. The ball is attached with uniformly rotating turn table (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.4).

blocks.text: A particle P moves round a circle of radius xo with uniform angular velocity w; its linear velocity at P is along the tangent, vp = xo w. Q is the projection of P on the diameter, and oscillates about the mean position O. If P starts at A, the angle swept in time t is theta = wt (Fig 14.5).

blocks.alt: A circle of radius xo with centre O and horizontal diameter ending at A. A point P on the circle moves anticlockwise with angular velocity omega; the radius OP makes the angle theta = omega t with OA. Q is the foot of the perpendicular from P on the diameter, and x = OQ is the displacement of Q from O.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.5: A point P moving on circular path at constant angular velocity (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.5).

items: Instantaneous displacement: in triangle POQ, OQ/OP = cos(theta), so x / xo = cos(wt) and x = xo cos(wt) (14.11).

Instantaneous velocity: the velocity of Q is the horizontal component of vp (Fig 14.6): v = vp cos(90 degrees - theta) = xo w sin(wt) (14.12). Using sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 and cos(theta) = x/xo, v = w square root of (xo^2 - x^2) = square root of [(k/m)(xo^2 - x^2)] (14.13). At the mean position x = 0, so the velocity is maximum: v_max = vo = xo w = square root of (k/m) xo (14.14).

blocks.alt: The same circle with diameter BA. At P the velocity vp points along the tangent. Its horizontal component v is drawn from P to R on the vertical diameter, parallel to BA, and an equal arrow v acts on Q along the diameter towards O. The angle between vp and the vertical is theta, and the angle between vp and PR is 90 degrees minus theta.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.6: Velocity of the point P and its horizontal component (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.6).

items: Instantaneous acceleration: the acceleration of P is centripetal, ap = xo w^2, towards the centre (Fig 14.7). The acceleration of Q is its horizontal component: a = -xo w^2 cos(theta) = -xo w^2 (x/xo), so a = -w^2 x (14.15). Since w is constant, a is proportional to -x: the condition for S.H.M.

blocks.alt: The same circle with points A, B and C. The centripetal acceleration ap of P points along PO towards the centre. Its horizontal component a acts on Q along the diameter BA towards O. The angle theta is marked at O and at P, and x is the distance OQ.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.7: Acceleration of the point P and its horizontal component (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.7).

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: The expressions for time period, displacement, velocity and acceleration that are true for the projection of a particle also apply to the particle moving in the circle.

A 0.2 kg mass is attached to a spring with k = 10 N m^-1. It is displaced 0.1 m from equilibrium and released from rest. Find (a) its acceleration and (b) its speed at x = 0.05 m. Solution: w = square root of (k/m) = square root of (10/0.2) = square root of 50, about 7.07 rad s^-1. (a) a = -w^2 x = -50 x 0.05 = -2.5 m s^-2. (b) v = w square root of (xo^2 - x^2) = 7.07 x square root of (0.01 - 0.0025) = 7.07 x 0.0866, about 0.612 m s^-1.
